tour.title: Project Overview
tour.description: Start with the project README to understand Jeeves as a productivity-focused GTD todos app built with Flutter (mobile/web/desktop) and FastAPI (Python backend), connected via PowerSync for offline-first bidirectional sync with PostgreSQL. The README maps out the mono-repo layout (app/, backend/, infra/) and describes the QA workflow via Firebase App Distribution, giving you the vocabulary and mental model for the rest of the tour.

tour.title: Flutter App Entry Point
tour.description: The main.dart file is where the Flutter app boots. It initializes notification services, seeds onboarding and shutdown state from SharedPreferences, handles notification action callbacks, and renders the root JeevesApp widget with Riverpod for state management and GoRouter for navigation. This single file reveals the app's runtime initialization sequence and the key dependencies it pulls in.
tour.languageLesson: Dart's top-level main() function is the app entry point. Flutter's runApp() takes a Widget tree root. Riverpod's ProviderScope wraps the entire app to enable dependency injection through providers that are lazily initialized and automatically disposed.

tour.title: Navigation and Routing
tour.description: The router is the highest fan-out file in the Flutter app, importing 18 screens and wiring them into a GoRouter configuration. It defines the complete screen hierarchy -- from authentication gates to the main app shell with inbox, next actions, focus sessions, periodic reviews, and settings. Reading this file gives you a map of every user-facing feature in the application.
tour.languageLesson: GoRouter uses declarative routing with redirect guards. The ShellRoute pattern wraps child routes in a persistent scaffold (bottom nav, app bar), so the app shell stays mounted while inner screens swap -- a common Flutter navigation pattern for tab-based layouts.

tour.title: Core Data Model and Database
tour.description: The GTD database is the most depended-upon file in the entire codebase (78 fan-in edges). It defines the Drift ORM schema with tables for todos, tags, focus sessions, time logs, and user preferences. The tables file declares the PowerSync-compatible schema with TEXT UUIDs, while the database class provides typed queries and DAOs. Nearly every provider and screen depends on this layer.
tour.languageLesson: Drift is a reactive persistence library for Dart that generates type-safe SQL queries at compile time. Tables are defined as Dart classes with typed columns, and DAOs (Data Access Objects) group related queries. Drift's watch() methods return Streams that automatically re-emit when underlying data changes, powering reactive UI updates.

tour.title: State Management Layer
tour.description: The providers layer sits between the database and the UI, exposing reactive state through Riverpod. The database provider (46 fan-in) is the second most imported file, while the focus session planning provider (27 fan-in) orchestrates the daily planning workflow. Together with auth, tags, inbox, and periodic review providers, this layer implements the GTD methodology as composable state machines.

tour.title: GTD Ceremonies and Rituals
tour.description: Jeeves structures productivity around three GTD ceremonies: Focus Session Planning (morning planning wizard), Periodic Review (weekly review steps), and Evening Shutdown (end-of-day ritual). Each ceremony is a multi-step wizard with its own provider managing state transitions. The planning screen walks users through energy check-in, inbox clarification, task review, and plan summary -- embodying GTD's 'getting control' workflow.

tour.title: Inbox and Task Processing
tour.description: The inbox is GTD's capture-and-clarify hub. The inbox screen displays unprocessed items with a quick-add bar for fast capture, while the clarify screen walks users through the 'process to' workflow -- deciding whether an item is actionable, delegatable, or deferrable. The clarify card and process-to handlers form a tightly coupled cluster (9 internal edges) that implements GTD's core decision tree.

tour.title: Sync Engine and Offline-First
tour.description: PowerSync provides bidirectional sync between the local Drift database and the PostgreSQL backend. The PowerSync provider manages the sync lifecycle, while the backend connector handles authentication token exchange and upload/download queues. The sync config YAML defines which tables replicate and how JWT-based client authentication works. This architecture enables the app to work fully offline and sync when connectivity returns.

tour.title: Backend API and Data Models
tour.description: The FastAPI backend serves as the sync target and API layer. Its main.py registers routers for health, auth, todos, tags, user preferences, AI suggestions, and PowerSync token endpoints. The SQLAlchemy models mirror the Flutter-side schema with TEXT UUIDs for PowerSync compatibility. The todo routes handle CRUD with tag filtering and resolution, while auth routes manage JWT token issuance for both password and SWS (Solana Wallet Signing) providers.

tour.title: Infrastructure and Local Dev
tour.description: The Docker Compose file orchestrates four local services: PostgreSQL (with logical replication for PowerSync), the PowerSync sync layer, the FastAPI backend, and Redis as a Celery broker. The backend Dockerfile builds a single-stage Python 3.14-slim image, while the Procfile defines Dokku deployment with Alembic migration on release. The Makefile ties everything together with developer workflow targets for setup, backend management, emulator launching, and cross-platform app running.
tour.languageLesson: Docker Compose's depends_on controls startup order but not readiness. PostgreSQL's logical replication (wal_level=logical) is required by PowerSync to stream row-level changes. The Procfile's release phase runs migrations before the web process starts, ensuring the database schema is current on every deploy.

tour.title: CI/CD Pipelines
tour.description: Six GitHub Actions workflows automate the entire delivery pipeline. Flutter CI runs analysis and tests on app/ changes, while Backend CI runs ruff linting, mypy, and pytest with a PostgreSQL service container. The app CD pipeline computes semantic versions, builds signed APKs for production and dev flavors, distributes to Firebase, and publishes to Google Play. Backend CD deploys to Dokku via SSH after CI passes on main. A PR-APK workflow builds debug APKs for pull request testing.
tour.languageLesson: GitHub Actions workflows use 'on' triggers with path filters to run only when relevant files change. The CD pipeline uses matrix-like flavor builds (production/dev) and conditional steps gated on branch name to separate staging from release distribution.

tour.title: Architecture and Requirements
tour.description: The architecture doc provides a comprehensive reference for the mono-repo's tech stack, platform I/O adapters, focus mode execution model, auth provider interface, and task domain model. The requirements doc defines the product vision across 11 epics -- from the GTD inventory engine and daily execution layer to AI-assisted triage and habit tracking. Together, these documents explain not just what the code does today, but where the project is heading.

tour.title: App Configuration and Dependencies
tour.description: The pubspec.yaml declares the Flutter app's dependency constellation: Riverpod for state management, Drift and PowerSync for offline-first sync, GoRouter for navigation, and flutter_local_notifications for ceremony nudges. The backend's pyproject.toml pins FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, Alembic, and PyJWT. The build.yaml configures Drift's code generator to use text-based datetime storage matching PowerSync's ISO-8601 serialization -- a subtle but critical alignment between the two data layers.
